title: I built an ASCII incremental horror game with an AI coding assistant. I'm still stunned at how good the end product became
author: BoredFourEternity
selftext:
I've spent about 6 months on and off building ANOMALY: The Nexus Protocol, an incremental horror game drawn entirely in ASCII, with Claude Code writing most of the code. It's on itch now with a free demo. Rather than just drop a link, here is what the process was actually like, including the parts that went badly.



The setup. It's a Rust project with the game rules, the content and the interface kept apart. All the story and balance live in plain text files (146 transmissions, 143 oracle answers, 63 upgrades and so on), so I could direct the writing and the numbers without touching code. There are no generated images or audio anywhere. The AI wrote code that draws every frame character by character and synthesises the sound at runtime. I tried AI-painted key art for the store page at one point and threw it out, because the script-drawn ASCII looked better and looked like the game.



What made the biggest difference: giving the AI ways to check its own work. Early on it would write an animation and tell me it looked good, having never seen it. So I had it build a tool that renders any animation frame by frame to images it can look at. The quality jumped as soon as it could see what it had drawn. Same idea for balance: there's a bot that plays the whole game headlessly, so pacing is measured instead of guessed.



Where it was confidently wrong. The bot finishes the first five cycles in about an hour. When I played it myself, the same stretch took me three and a half hours, and resources felt far too generous. The bot plays perfectly and never reads anything, so everything tuned against it was tuned for a player who doesn't exist. I've since added a record inside the save file of what a real player unlocked and when, so the next balance pass uses real play.



It also once "improved" a cutscene after judging the original from a thumbnail-sized contact sheet. The new one was worse. I had it put the old one back. The lesson for me was that it will act on a weak look at something as confidently as on a careful one, and it's my job to ask how it knows.



What stayed mine. The story, the canon, what's frightening and what isn't, and every call on feel. The lore was worked out over long back-and-forth conversations where I rejected most of the first ideas. The AI is a very fast pair of hands and a decent sounding board. It is not a designer, and it doesn't know when something is boring.



Happy to go into detail on any of it: the test setup, how the content files are organised, how the ASCII rendering works, or what I'd do differently.



Trailer: [https://youtu.be/FODk0KQyi8E](https://youtu.be/FODk0KQyi8E)

Game and free demo: [https://netherglow.itch.io/anomaly](https://netherglow.itch.io/anomaly) ($4.99, Windows and Linux)
